section.title: Paying for it
section.intro: Most of what college costs can be reduced or covered, and one route even pays you while you learn. Every year people miss out on help they would have got, just because they didn't know it was there.

items.title: HEAR
items.subtitle: Higher Education Access Route
items.summary: A way into college on reduced points if your circumstances qualify. A lot of the students it was set up for never apply.
items.body:
HEAR offers college places on reduced points, plus extra support once you're in, to school leavers from socio-economically disadvantaged backgrounds. The universities run it through the CAO.

There's a real chance you qualify. It's assessed on your household, so you need to apply and show your circumstances rather than hoping someone notices them.

This might be the most useful thing on this website. Every year people who would have qualified miss out. It's nearly always for one of three reasons: nobody mentioned it, the paperwork looked like too much, or they assumed it was meant for someone worse off.

blocks.heading: What you actually get
blocks.text: A place on lower points than the published requirement, and support once you're there, such as orientation, study help and in some cases money. It's not a lesser degree. It's the same course, the same exams and the same degree, and nobody can tell afterwards.

blocks.heading: The deadline is earlier than you think
blocks.text: HEAR goes in with your CAO application, but its closing date is well before the main CAO one. Supporting documents are due even earlier. Miss it and you'll have to wait a year. Look up this year's dates in the autumn of sixth year, not in the spring.

blocks.heading: The paperwork is the real hurdle
blocks.text: You'll need proof of income and evidence of your circumstances. None of it is hard, it's just tedious, and that's what puts people off. Start early and ask your guidance counsellor to help. It's exactly what they're there for, and most will be glad you asked.

blocks.heading: Applying costs you nothing
blocks.text: If it turns out you're not eligible, your normal CAO application carries on as usual. Applying can't leave you worse off.

myths.myth: It's for people in real hardship, not me.
myths.reality: It looks at several things, not just income, and plenty of ordinary working households qualify. Let them decide if you're eligible. Don't rule yourself out.

myths.myth: Everyone will know I got in on reduced points.
myths.reality: They won't. It isn't on your degree and nobody in your lectures is told.
You handle it. The school can help with documents, but nobody will do it for you or chase you to get it done.

items.title: SUSI
items.subtitle: The grant
items.summary: Covers fees for a lot of students and pays a maintenance grant to some. The most common mistake is assuming you won't qualify and never checking.
items.body:
SUSI is the national student grant. Depending on your household income and circumstances, it can cover your student contribution and also pay you a maintenance grant to live on.

The income limits are higher than most people guess, and applying is free. Plenty of students end up paying for something they would have got, just because they assumed they were over the limit and never checked.

blocks.heading: Two separate things
blocks.text: One part covers your fees and the other pays you money to live on. They're assessed separately, so you might get one and not the other, and the maintenance grant is higher if college is far from home.

blocks.heading: Apply before you know where you're going
blocks.text: You don't need an offer to apply. If you wait until August, you'll be waiting on money you need in September, along with everyone else.

blocks.heading: There's other money too
blocks.text: Most colleges run a Student Assistance Fund for students hit by costs they didn't see coming. It's discretionary and confidential, and far fewer people use it than could. Ask the access office about it in your first week, before you need it.

myths.reality: Maybe, but the limits surprise people and they change every year. Check before you rule yourself out.
There's also a maintenance grant, and it's paid directly to you.
